Folio 21r has no derivation and no new mathematics. It is the right-hand strip of the same sheet as the previous page: a fold or partial scan shows only the ends of the lines of the 'Zusatz zu pag. 1'. The ink line-ends match the previous page line for line: 'z än-[dert sich]', '[x]=b', 'unend-[lich kleinen]', 'Ände-[rung]', 'belie-[big]', 'so', 'welches', '> ε ist.' The pencil lines below likewise end the pencil paragraph of the previous page: '[d]iesen', '[...] die zu Art. 3. citirte, und', '[gen]erales', a struck-through '[Com]ment.' (from 'Comment. Gott. rec. T. VI'), and '[zu] verweisen'. The '21' in the right margin is the archival foliation.

Content of the full note (reconstructed from both images; the definitional reading is mine):
(1) Definition: z varies continuously with x on [a,b] if every infinitely small change of x gives an infinitely small change of z. More tangibly: for every ε>0 there is α>0 such that, inside any x-interval of length < α, the difference of two values of z never exceeds ε. In modern terms this is the oscillation form of uniform continuity on [a,b]: for all ε there is α such that |x1−x2|<α implies |z(x1)−z(x2)|≤ε.
(2) Consequence: continuity so defined implies that z stays finite (bounded) on the interval. This is correct. Cover [a,b] by finitely many intervals of length < α; then |z(x)−z(a)| ≤ ε·ceil((b−a)/α).
(3) A pencil bibliographic remark refers the reader to the work cited at Art. 3 and to Gauss, Disquisitiones generales circa superficies curvas, art. 13. The deleted words show the place of publication (Comment. Gott. rec. T. VI) being struck.

Context: this is a draft supplement to Riemann's 1851 dissertation 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse'. Art. 1 there treats continuity, and Art. 3 cites Gauss on conformal representation. The next page ('Wir betrachten ein Abhängigkeitsgesetz als desto einfacher...') also belongs to dissertation drafts.
errors: No mathematical errors. Boundedness does follow, because the definition is uniform: one α serves the whole interval [a,b].
Nothing on this page can be checked independently; it is a fragment of line endings.

results.what: ε–α definition of continuity of a function on an interval, in oscillation form (any two values within an x-interval of length < α differ by at most ε)
results.modern_name: uniform continuity (ε–δ definition) on a closed interval
results.usually_credited_to: Bolzano (1817) and Cauchy (1821) in infinitesimal/limit form; ε–δ rigour usually credited to Weierstrass (lectures, 1850s–60s); the uniform-continuity distinction to Heine (1872)

results.what: Continuity (in the above sense) implies boundedness on the interval
results.modern_name: boundedness of uniformly continuous functions on bounded intervals

results.what: Reference to Gauss, Disquisitiones generales circa superficies curvas art. 13, and to the work cited at dissertation Art. 3 (Gauss's conformal-mapping essay)

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds only line endings of a note fully visible on the previous page. That note gives an ε–α (uniform) definition of continuity in a draft for the 1851 dissertation. This is mildly interesting as an early ε-formulation, but it is routine in content. Riemann's use of oscillation-style conditions (e.g. in the 1854 Habilitation on trigonometric series) is well known.

checkable.sympy: Abs(z(x1)-z(a)) <= ceiling((b-a)/alpha)*epsilon  # informal: chain of steps of length < alpha
checkable.asserts: Uniform ε–α continuity on [a,b] bounds |z| by |z(a)| + ε·ceil((b−a)/α), so continuity implies finiteness
